title: A Receptor Waits Off DNA or On It

scenes.tts: What does a receptor do before its hormone arrives? The family has two answers. The first is a chaperone. The glucocorticoid and androgen receptors wait mostly in the cytoplasm, held by chaperones built around H S P 90. A chaperone is a protein that helps other proteins hold their shape. Here it keeps the pocket ready for hormone, and keeps the receptor off D N A. When hormone binds, the receptor is released and moves into the nucleus. There it pairs with a second copy of itself and binds its response elements.

Here it keeps the pocket ready for hormone, and keeps the receptor off DNA. When hormone binds, the receptor is released and moves into the nucleus. scenes.visual: A cell with cytoplasm and nucleus. A blue receptor with an open pocket sits in the cytoplasm wrapped in purple H S P 90 chaperone chips, far from the DNA in the nucleus. A yellow hormone dot binds the pocket, the chaperones drop away, the receptor moves into the nucleus, a second copy joins it and the pair sits on two response elements on the DNA.
scenes.narration: What does a receptor do before its hormone arrives? The family has two answers. The first is a chaperone. The glucocorticoid and androgen receptors wait mostly in the cytoplasm, held by chaperones built around HSP90. A chaperone is a protein that helps other proteins hold their shape. Here it keeps the pocket ready for hormone, and keeps the receptor off DNA. When hormone binds, the receptor is released and moves into the nucleus. scenes.tts: The second answer is to wait on the D N A. The receptors for thyroid hormone, retinoic acid and vitamin D stay in the nucleus, and so do the P P A R receptors. They bind D N A paired with a partner from the same family called R X R. Their two half sites point the same way. The gap between them helps decide which pair fits: one base for P P A R, three for vitamin D, four for thyroid hormone, five for retinoic acid.
scenes.caption: The second answer is to wait on the DNA. The receptors for thyroid hormone, retinoic acid and vitamin D stay in the nucleus, and so do the PPAR receptors. The gap between them helps decide which pair fits: one base for PPAR, three for vitamin D, four for thyroid hormone, five for retinoic acid.
scenes.visual: Inside a nucleus outline, four rows. Each has a receptor name, then plus R X R in orange, then DNA with two half-site arrows pointing the same way and a gap of base squares: one, three, four, five.

scenes.tts: Without hormone, the thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors hold co-repressors, proteins that keep the gene off. Hormone releases the co-repressor and brings in its place a co-activator, a protein that helps switch the gene on.

scenes.visual: A receptor pair on a response element, red co-repressors on it, the gene red and off. A yellow hormone arrives, the co-repressors leave, green co-activators take their place and the gene turns green and on.

scenes.tts: An empty receptor of this kind is an active off. A gene carrying an empty thyroid hormone receptor is quieter than the same gene with no receptor at all. So a receptor can wait off the D N A, or wait on it.
